newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladeshis return home from UAE to uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Bangladeshis return home from UAE to uncertainty.

text.p: Hundreds of Bangladeshis who arrived in Dhaka on Monday from the United Arab Emirates leaving behind their jobs said they faced an uncertain future back home.

The exodus has been triggered by a new immigration law in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which comes into effect on October 1, imposing stiff penalties on illegal aliens or workers who violate labour laws.

"We have been driven away like cats and dogs," said Oli Miah of northeastern Sylhet district. "I had worked there for five or six years without any papers...but was suddenly told I am an outlaw and illegal immigrant," he told reporters at the airport.
His companion Farid Miah said he worked in the Gulf state for three years, but no one had asked him for any documentation until this month.
"Things are happening too fast and many of the deportees have not been able to take their belongings and money from banks," said Abdur Rahman of Chittagong district.
They were among 250 Bangladeshi workers flown to Dhaka on Monday by Gulf Air. At least three other flights from different airlines were expected later in the day.
Airport officials said over 2,700 workers returned to Dhaka between Thursday and Sunday, and they expect a similar number to come home on Monday.

Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad said on Saturday that nearly 30,000 Bangladeshis who worked in the UAE without valid permits or overstayed would be required to return home under the new immigration law.
He said the government had no plan to compensate the returnees.
"Those coming back have the ability to buy their tickets and possibly to set up a living back home. They have all worked there for years and have savings," the minister said.
The UAE has given a two-month amnesty to illegal workers during which they must get their papers in order or leave.
Diplomats expect some 200,000 expatriates will have left by the end of the August-September amnesty period.
Dhaka officials said on Monday they were not sure if all the 30,000 Bangladeshis could be brought back by the September 30 deadline despite contingency plans.
